figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: One object over one century. Wikimedia Commons holds 727 photos of the locomotive Flying Scotsman, taken from the 1920s to 2026 by 187 photographers using 123 camera models. The twelve photos on the left are labeled with their year and camera; our recovered sparse point cloud and camera poses are shown on the right. Trainspotting contains 12,068 such objects reconstructed from 311,886 photos from Wikimedia Commons. We use this dataset to substantially improve feedforward 3D reconstruction models on in-the-wild object-centric photo collections.
figures.headline: The 727 Flying Scotsman photos on Commons, spanning the 1920s to 2026, reconstruct into one shared sparse point cloud and camera poses.
citing_sentences: Figure 1 shows an example of such photos, depicting the locomotive Flying Scotsman captured over a century in many different locations.
An example reconstruction of the Flying Scotsman is shown on the right of Figure 1.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: VGGT-$\Omega$ fails on the Buick Riviera. We visualize the camera poses and point map predicted by VGGT-$\Omega$ from sixteen photos of the Buick Riviera (multiple physical instances of the same car design). The views are misregistered and the car is reconstructed as scattered fragments. Figure 6 shows the reconstruction of our fine-tuned model from the same photos.
figures.headline: VGGT-Ω misregisters sixteen Buick Riviera photos, so the car is reconstructed as scattered fragments.
citing_sentences: Standard reconstruction pipelines are unreliable in such in-the-wild settings, and so are feedforward reconstruction models, which are largely trained on their output (Figure 2).

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Examples of capture variation. Each column displays photos of example objects, grouped into the three regimes (fixed, roaming, and instance-pooled) and labeled with their year and camera. Fixed objects stay at one site, roaming objects are single instances that move between sites, and instance-pooled objects are different physical instances of one shared design.
figures.headline: Objects fall into fixed, roaming, and instance-pooled regimes, each with a different kind of variation across photos.
citing_sentences: We denote these distinct categories as fixed, roaming, and instance-pooled (Figure 3).

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Reconstruction pipeline for the Flying Scotsman. (a) Object gating retains 570 of 727 photos, with red borders marking excluded photos. (b) A retrieved pair is shown with candidate correspondences. Green correspondences pass the confidence, cycle, and epipolar checks, while dashed red correspondences fail. (c) The structure-from-motion reconstruction registers 496 images, merged from 14 partial reconstructions. View selection keeps 481 of them for multi-view stereo. (d) The same pair shows MVS depth before and after MoGe-2 filtering. (e) Four of the 370 photos in the dataset show MVS depth in color and the selected mask in teal over the image.
figures.headline: The pipeline keeps 570 of 727 Flying Scotsman photos and registers 496 of them in the structure from motion reconstruction.
citing_sentences: Figure 4 follows one object through the reconstruction pipeline.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Object statistics by regime. Distributions over Trainspotting of the number of photos, the span of capture dates, the number of photographers, and the number of camera models.
figures.headline: Per-regime distributions show how photo count, capture span, photographers, and camera models vary across Trainspotting objects.
citing_sentences: Figure 5 shows these distributions by regime.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Qualitative comparison. We visualize ground truth and predicted camera poses and point maps from $\pi^{3}$ [52], Depth Anything 3 [25], VGGT-$\Omega$ [49], and Spotter on held out objects from Trainspotting and NAVI in-the-wild [19]. We use 4 or 16 input views for Trainspotting and 8 for NAVI in-the-wild. Only the first 4 input views are shown. Triangular markers indicate the directions of the cameras outside of the frame. The baselines misregister the input views and produce duplicated or fragmented geometry, whereas Spotter recovers a single consistent object and accurate camera poses.
figures.headline: On held-out samples, Spotter recovers one consistent object where the baselines misregister views and produce fragmented geometry.
citing_sentences: Figure 6 shows reconstructions of four Trainspotting objects and two NAVI in-the-wild objects.

figures.label: Figure S1
figures.caption: Structure from motion with other matchers. Each row shows one Trainspotting object: six of the input photos, then the largest model of COLMAP with SIFT, SuperPoint with LightGlue, MASt3R matches with the COLMAP mapper, MASt3R-SfM, and our pipeline, all run on the same images. The number of registered images out of the input images is given under each panel. The other methods fail on instance-pooled and roaming objects, and on fixed objects our pipeline produces a more complete and cleaner reconstruction. In the bottom three rows, we frame the object to show its details, so not all cameras are visible.
figures.headline: Alternative matchers fail on instance-pooled and roaming objects, while the paper's pipeline gives more complete fixed-object reconstructions.
citing_sentences: Figure S1 compares the pipeline of Section 4 of the main paper with four alternatives on the images that pass object gating: COLMAP with SIFT and exhaustive matching [30, 35], SuperPoint with LightGlue [11, 26] in hloc [33] with NetVLAD retrieval [3], MASt3R matches [22] with the COLMAP mapper, and MASt3R-SfM [13].

figures.label: Figure S2
figures.caption: Failure cases. Four held-out samples on which Spotter fails: airliner (noisy depth at long focal lengths), car (misregistered close-up of a wheel), grave monument (doppelganger ambiguity), and toy shark from NAVI in-the-wild (out of distribution).
figures.headline: Four held-out samples show failures from noisy depth at long focal lengths, misregistered close-ups, doppelganger ambiguity, and out-of-distribution input.
citing_sentences: Figure S2 shows four held-out samples on which Spotter fails, one for each of the most common failure modes.

figures.label: Figure S3
figures.caption: Additional qualitative comparisons. Ten held-out samples drawn at random: three Trainspotting objects with 16 input views, five with 4 input views, and two NAVI in-the-wild objects with 8 input views.
figures.headline: Ten randomly drawn held-out samples compare predicted cameras and point maps across Trainspotting and NAVI in-the-wild objects.

abstract: State-of-the-art feedforward reconstruction models perform poorly on in-the-wild object-centric photo collections. They are trained largely on single-session object captures whose images vary in viewpoint while the object and its environment remain nearly fixed. Public photo archives contain a different form of multi-view data. They hold found photos of the same object or design: photos taken independently by many people across years, environments, cameras, and sometimes physical units. In this work, we introduce Trainspotting, a dataset of 12,068 objects and 311,886 photos from Wikimedia Commons. We reconstruct each object to recover camera poses, multi-view stereo depth, and object masks. We categorize the objects into three regimes: objects fixed at one site, objects that move between sites, and designs shared by many physical units. Evaluating recent feedforward reconstruction models on Trainspotting shows that they fail most severely in the last two regimes. Fine-tuning VGGT-$\Omega$ on Trainspotting significantly improves camera pose, depth, and 3D geometry on held-out objects. We observe similar improvements on the independent NAVI in-the-wild benchmark, which contains photos of each object in different environments. Performance on conventional benchmarks remains largely unchanged.

sections.body: Wikimedia Commons holds found photos of objects such as locomotives, statues, and car models, taken by many people over many years. Viewpoints are unevenly sampled, environments change between photos, and photos of a design may show different physical units. Classical structure from motion and feedforward models both struggle with such collections. The authors build a reconstruction pipeline and release Trainspotting, with 12,068 objects and 311,886 photos paired with camera poses, multi-view stereo depth, and object masks. They fine-tune VGGT-Ω on it to produce Spotter. Spotter raises camera-pose area under the accuracy curve at 30 degrees (AUC@30) from 25 to 81 on held-out objects and from 19 to 76 on NAVI in-the-wild.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Public archives hold many found photos of one object, but feedforward reconstruction models are trained mostly on single-session captures.

sections.body: CO3D, uCO3D, and MVImgNet record each object in a single capture lasting minutes. NAVI photographs each object in different environments, but it contains only 36 objects, and its images are aligned to 3D models by hand. MegaDepth, MegaScenes, and MegaDepth-X reconstruct internet photos, but they target scenes. Of the 12,068 Trainspotting objects, only 1,163 (9.6%) are reconstructed as scenes in MegaScenes and 56 (0.5%) in MegaDepth-X, mostly objects installed at one site. The related work also covers learned matchers, and the pipeline uses RoMa v2 for dense correspondences.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Existing object datasets record each object in one capture, and internet photo reconstructions cover mostly scenes.

sections.body: Each object corresponds to one Wikimedia Commons category, and its images form a collection. The traversal of the category graph records 155,744 categories. A large language model classifies each category from its title and parent categories. It keeps rigid physical objects, labels each as an individual or a design, and marks whether it is permanently installed at one site. These labels set the regime of each object. The classifier yields 33,884 candidate objects, and 17,470 are attempted after filtering on photo count. The text states that the regime labels are approximate. 68% of the objects have a Wikidata item.
sections.heading: The Trainspotting Dataset
sections.headline: Language-model classification of Wikimedia Commons categories yields 12,068 rigid objects, each labeled fixed, roaming, or instance-pooled.

sections.body: Object gating uses SAM3, prompted with a text prompt written by a large language model, to keep photos where the largest detection covers at least 10% of the image. RoMa v2 correspondences are kept only if their certainty passes a threshold and they pass forward-backward cycle and epipolar checks. The matches are linked into multi-view tracks and reconstructed incrementally with COLMAP. A view is kept only if enough of its points have track length at least three. Depth comes from Cas-DiffMVS and is checked against MoGe-2 monocular depth. Structure from motion succeeds for 85% of objects and registers 72% of gated photos. Held-out Trainspotting scores are measured against these reconstructions, not independent ground truth.
sections.heading: Pseudo-Ground Truth via Reconstruction
sections.headline: A dense-matching pipeline with geometric checks recovers camera poses, depth, and masks for each object as pseudo-ground truth.

sections.body: Spotter fine-tunes the released 1B-parameter VGGT-Ω checkpoint on the training objects, updating the camera head and all attention blocks. Training combines camera, depth, and point losses, with 15% of each batch replayed from BlendedMVS, Hypersim, and uCO3D, for 7,500 steps. On 1,635 held-out Trainspotting samples, Spotter has the lowest point-map accuracy error (1.22) and completeness error (1.15) in Table 3. Its AUC@30 is 81.2, against 25.0 for VGGT-Ω. Fine-tuning changes AUC@30 on conventional benchmarks by at most 1.1 points relative to VGGT-Ω. The depth inlier ratio is measured after a single median scale per sample.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Fine-tuning lifts held-out camera-pose score at the 30-degree threshold from 25.0 to 81.2 and depth inlier ratio from 28.1 to 53.3.

sections.body: The conclusion restates that base models trained mainly on single-session captures perform poorly on in-the-wild object collections. It argues that Trainspotting turns found photos into training data at scale. The authors state that training on fixed objects alone transfers poorly to roaming and instance-pooled objects, so what the base models lacked was variation in how an object is photographed. The section also proposes Trainspotting as a benchmark for reconstruction under changing environments, and as a source for studying how objects change over time. It reports no new experiments for these uses, so the claims rest on the earlier results.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Variation in how an object is photographed, not only dataset scale, is what the base models lacked.

sections.body: The appendix gives the 53 object categories with their object and photo counts (Table S1), reasons for rejecting 8,956 categories (Table S2), and the overlap with MegaScenes and MegaDepth-X by regime (Table S3). It reports the yield at each reconstruction stage, from 17,470 input objects to 12,068 in the final dataset (Table S4), and the pipeline thresholds (Table S5). The pipeline is compared with COLMAP using SIFT, SuperPoint with LightGlue, and MASt3R matches, and the alternatives fail on instance-pooled and roaming objects. It also gives training settings, the evaluation protocol for samples and external datasets, and an intersection over union of 0.92 for the object mask head on held-out objects.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: Appendix lists category counts, rejected categories, pipeline yields, matcher comparison, thresholds, training, and evaluation details.
